newsitem.title: USA: Cleveland Fed conference favors target for Fed.
newsitem.headline: Cleveland Fed conference favors target for Fed.

text.p: Most participants at a Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland conference advocated specific numerical targets as a guide to Fed monetary policy.
That approach, already supported by some Fed officials, would clearly state policy goals, enhance transparency and hold the central bank more accountable for the outcome of its policy, they said.
The Cleveland Fed conference on the "Dynamic Effects of Monetary Policy" was held November 7-8.
However, the participants were split between targeting an inflation gauge or the nominal Gross Domestic Product.

Since the performance of the U.S. monetary aggregates is no longer a reliable indicator of inflationary pressures and thus not a guide to Fed policy, the economists advocated targeting either the Consumer Price Index or nominal GDP -- two gauges of the impact of monetary policy on the economy.

Many conference participants also rejected the relevance of the non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment (NAIRU) therory as a guide for monetary policy, pointing out there is no tight relationship between unemployment and inflation.
According to the current Keynesian school of economists, inflation should pick up when the U.S. unemployment rate is at or below 5.75 percent over an extended period of time.
However, the jobless rate has been at or below 5.8 percent since September 1994 and price pressures have not emerged.

"The last 1-1/2 years show how little confidence we should have in the estimates of NAIRU and policies based on NAIRU. It's simply not a reliable guide to policy," Northwestern University economics professor Marty Eichenbaum told Reuters.
"We now understand the monetary policy transmission mechanism a lot better than we did 10 years ago," he added.
Eichenbaum said he favors a "gross domestic product-like target because it will help bring inflation down while allowing monetary policy to accommodate shocks."

St. Louis Fed vice president Bill Gavin said one main result of the conference -- similar to the outcome of a recent St. Louis Fed conference -- is that the behavior of money has wrested the spotlight away from growth in economists' theories about conducting monetary policy.
Gavin said adopting a numerical target would be an important step for the Fed to take in order to further establish its credibility.
"The one issue the participants did not address is when the intention of the central bank is uncertain," Gavin said.

"In their models (presented at the conference), the central bank has an explicit target," Gavin added. "It's very different to get a solution if the central bank's intention is not clearly expressed."

Lee Ohanian, assistant professor of economics at the University of Minnesota and the University of Pennsylvania, noted "the most important finding is that higher-than-expected growth does not lead to higher inflation."
Ohanian agreed "a choice of targets for Fed policy is key," mainly because charting policy based on inflation expectations tied to growth "can lead to very poor policy outcome."
Ohanian also said numerical targets would serve Fed policy well in a low-inflation environment where the motivation for policy moves is often unclear to financial markets.

"Numerical targets seem the best objective given the biases in the CPI and would make it look reasonable for the Fed to reduce inflation to the smallest possible number," Ohanian concluded. "There is little benefit in reducing inflation below 2.0 percent because we don't know large is the bias in the CPI."
New York Fed President William McDonough was the first senior Fed official to propose targeting CPI between 0.5 percent and 2.0 percent.
